title: Proving Which Kinase Did the Work

scenes.visual: Full-frame 16:9 dark charcoal lab bench reusing film 1's exact colour map: slate grey = bystander kinases, gold = target kinase X and its substrate, emerald green = phosphate, cyan = bulky labelled ATP analog, coral red = chemical inhibitor. A cluster of slate kinase blocks surrounds one gold kinase X, all sharing similarly shaped ATP notches. Title 'Proving Which Kinase Did the Work' fades in cleanly over the pulsing kinase grid.

scenes.tts: The first film showed how antibodies and mass spectrometry find one phosphate among thousands of proteins. Finding that mark is only half the problem. Roughly five hundred human kinases share a similar A T P pocket. How do you prove which kinase added it, and caused the response?
scenes.caption: The first film showed how antibodies and mass spectrometry find one phosphate among thousands of proteins. Finding that mark is only half the problem. Roughly 500 human kinases share a similar ATP pocket. How do you prove which kinase added it, and caused the response?
scenes.visual: Right zone shows film 1's gold protein with an emerald phosphate dot ('Phosphorylated target, schematic'). Left and center zones expand into dozens of slate kinase blocks around one gold kinase X, all with similar ATP pocket notches (badge '~500 human kinases'). Question holds cleanly at top: 'Which kinase added it, and did it cause the response?'
scenes.narration: The first film showed how antibodies and mass spectrometry find one phosphate among thousands of proteins. Finding that mark is only half the problem. Roughly 500 human kinases share a similar ATP pocket. How do you prove which kinase added it, and caused the response?

scenes.tts: Two obvious tests both fail to find direct targets. Add ordinary radioactive A T P to an extract, and every active kinase labels its substrates at once. Or remove kinase X from cells. Phosphorylation drops on direct targets and on proteins three steps downstream, looking identical.
scenes.caption: Two obvious tests both fail to find direct targets. Add ordinary radioactive ATP to an extract, and every active kinase labels its substrates at once. Or remove kinase X from cells. Phosphorylation drops on direct targets and on proteins three steps downstream, looking identical.
scenes.visual: Left-to-right pathway bench ('Schematic'): first, cyan ordinary ATP flies into both gold kinase X and every slate kinase, lighting up a crowd of targets at once. Next, gold kinase X dims and is crossed out; a chain of three downstream slate steps (X -> K2 -> K3 -> Target) all lose emerald phosphate dots together, making direct and indirect targets indistinguishable.
scenes.narration: Two obvious tests both fail to find direct targets. Add ordinary radioactive ATP to an extract, and every active kinase labels its substrates at once. Or remove kinase X from cells. Phosphorylation drops on direct targets and on proteins three steps downstream, looking identical.

scenes.tts: Kevan Shokat's laboratory solved this by reshaping one kinase's pocket. In a normal kinase, a bulky gatekeeper residue narrows the A T P pocket. Mutate that gatekeeper in kinase X to small glycine or alanine, opening a hole. Now supply a bulky benzyl A T P analog carrying a radioactive gamma phosphate.
scenes.caption: Kevan Shokat's laboratory solved this by reshaping one kinase's pocket. In a normal kinase, a bulky gatekeeper residue narrows the ATP pocket. Mutate that gatekeeper in kinase X to small glycine or alanine, opening a hole. Now supply a bulky benzyl ATP analog carrying a radioactive gamma phosphate.
scenes.visual: Zoom on gold kinase X beside a normal slate kinase ('Schematic pockets, not molecular structures'). A protruding slate bump ('Gatekeeper') inside gold kinase X shrinks away ('Gly / Ala'), carving an extra recess in its ATP cleft. A cyan-tagged bulky ATP cartoon ('Bulky benzyl on adenine' + emerald 'Gamma phosphate') approaches both pockets.
scenes.narration: Kevan Shokat's laboratory solved this by reshaping one kinase's pocket. In a normal kinase, a bulky gatekeeper residue narrows the ATP pocket. Mutate that gatekeeper in kinase X to small glycine or alanine, opening a hole. Now supply a bulky benzyl ATP analog carrying a radioactive gamma phosphate.

scenes.tts: The bulky benzyl group fits normal pockets poorly, so other kinases keep using ordinary A T P silently. Only engineered, analog-sensitive kinase X accepts the bulky analog and transfers its radioactive phosphate to direct substrates. The bulky group stays behind on adenine; only the phosphate moves.
scenes.caption: The bulky benzyl group fits normal pockets poorly, so other kinases keep using ordinary ATP silently. Only engineered, analog-sensitive kinase X accepts the bulky analog and transfers its radioactive phosphate to direct substrates. The bulky group stays behind on adenine; only the phosphate moves.
scenes.visual: The bulky cyan ATP analog bounces off the tight slate kinase pocket, then docks smoothly into gold kinase X's enlarged recess. The emerald radioactive gamma phosphate transfers onto a gold substrate block, while the cyan benzyl-ADP piece drifts away unused. Label 'Direct substrate candidate' lights up beside the gold substrate.
scenes.narration: The bulky benzyl group fits normal pockets poorly, so other kinases keep using ordinary ATP silently. Only engineered, analog-sensitive kinase X accepts the bulky analog and transfers its radioactive phosphate to direct substrates. The bulky group stays behind on adenine; only the phosphate moves.

scenes.tts: Next, test whether kinase X actually causes the cell's response. Labs often add a chemical inhibitor that plugs the A T P pocket. Because hundreds of kinases share that pocket, selectivity is hard to achieve. Large panel surveys found that many widely used inhibitors hit several kinases, not just the one they are sold for.
scenes.caption: Next, test whether kinase X actually causes the cell's response. Labs often add a chemical inhibitor that plugs the ATP pocket. Because hundreds of kinases share that pocket, selectivity is hard to achieve. Large panel surveys found that many widely used inhibitors hit several kinases, not just the one they are sold for.
scenes.visual: Zoom back to the kinase panel with an emerald response meter on the right. Coral-red wedges ('ATP-pocket inhibitor') plug gold kinase X plus ten surrounding slate kinases at once. Clean on-screen summary ('Published panel surveys'): '65 inhibitors vs 70–80 kinases (2007)' and '38 inhibitors vs 317 kinases (2008)' with coral off-target markers lighting across the panel.
scenes.narration: Next, test whether kinase X actually causes the cell's response. Labs often add a chemical inhibitor that plugs the ATP pocket. Because hundreds of kinases share that pocket, selectivity is hard to achieve. Large panel surveys found that many widely used inhibitors hit several kinases, not just the one they are sold for.

scenes.tts: That makes an unselective inhibitor one-sided. If X and many other kinases are shut off, yet the response survives, X is ruled out. If the response stops, X or any off-target could be responsible. Express a drug-resistant mutant of X. If the response returns while off-targets stay blocked, the drug acted through X.

scenes.visual: Three smooth transformations on the same kinase panel and response meter ('Schematic'): (1) Coral wedges plug gold X + slate kinases, emerald response bar stays FULL -> badge 'X not needed (ruled out)'. (2) Coral wedges plug gold X + slate kinases, response bar drops to ZERO -> '?' hovers over X and slate kinases ('Ambiguous'). (3) Gold X swaps to 'Drug-resistant X'; coral wedge bounces off gold X while all slate kinases stay plugged, and the response bar refills -> badge 'Drug acted through X (direct link not yet shown)'.
scenes.narration: That makes an unselective inhibitor one-sided. If X and many other kinases are shut off, yet the response survives, X is ruled out. If the response stops, X or any off-target could be responsible. Express a drug-resistant mutant of X. If the response returns while off-targets stay blocked, the drug acted through X.

scenes.tts: Two words organise every causal test: necessary and sufficient. A step is necessary if removing it stops the response. It is sufficient if turning it on alone triggers the response without hormone. Suppose an always-active kinase X triggers the full response without hormone. Does that prove X is necessary when hormone arrives?
scenes.caption: Two words organise every causal test: necessary and sufficient. A step is necessary if removing it stops the response. It is sufficient if turning it on alone triggers the response without hormone. Suppose an always-active kinase X triggers the full response without hormone. Does that prove X is necessary when hormone arrives?
scenes.visual: Left hormone badge switches OFF ('No hormone'). Gold kinase X glows bright ('Always-active X') and drives the right-zone emerald response bar to FULL. Question banner holds cleanly at top: 'Always-active X triggers response without hormone. Is X necessary for the hormone?'
scenes.narration: Two words organise every causal test: necessary and sufficient. A step is necessary if removing it stops the response. It is sufficient if turning it on alone triggers the response without hormone. Suppose an always-active kinase X triggers the full response without hormone. Does that prove X is necessary when hormone arrives?

scenes.visual: Hold the question banner, 'No hormone' badge, glowing always-active gold kinase X, and full emerald response meter on screen. A gentle cyan progress bar sweeps along the bottom for 4.5 seconds while subtle energy pulses travel from X to the meter.

scenes.tts: No, because when hormone arrives, a parallel pathway could still drive the response without X. Turning X on alone shows it is sufficient, not necessary. Every method fails in its own way: inhibitors hit off-targets, and knockouts disrupt whole networks. Causal claims earn belief when two methods that fail differently agree.

scenes.visual: Hormone turns ON, gold kinase X is crossed out, and a parallel slate pathway illuminates from hormone to the emerald response meter, keeping it FULL ('Sufficient is not necessary'). Then two independent method badges—'Drug-resistant rescue' (coral/gold) and 'Genetic knockout or site mutant' (emerald/violet)—converge with matching checkmarks onto one causal arrow.
